task: # RE-SCOPED 2026-08-13 (superset of the original cross-site framing; existing gold remains valid). compare candidate products against explicit criteria and constraints before buying: state what matters (budget, must-have features, dietary/size/spec constraints, ratings), search or filter to the candidates that satisfy them, compare the shortlist side by side — on one site's compare/filter tools or across sites (retailers, review sites, price trackers) — and reach a justified pick; complete when a pick is settled with the comparing evidence on screen (the chosen option over the compared candidates or the applied filters). Surface pinned: shopping/review sites' search, filter, and compare features in a browser or app. Variants: reseller/arbitrage product research (sourcing to resell for profit), dropshipping content, B2B pricing-tool demos, and talking-head opinion videos without screen evidence do not belong.

questions.check: Does the compare table have a blank or 'N/A' cell in a row that matches one of the person's stated must-have constraints?

children.label: Read the site's score and reasons

questions.question: How do the site's overall scores compare for the two phones?
questions.why: Seeing that both phones scored 59 points but have specific advantages like higher pixel density or CPU speed helps you understand the high-level tradeoffs before diving into detailed specs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally weigh which specific summary advantages, like a faster CPU or better camera, matter most to you when the overall scores are tied.

questions.question: How does the added phone score, and does the site badge it the winner?

questions.say_example: The site marks <the phone you just added> as Comparison Winner, <81> against <62> for the other two. That badge is the site's scoring.

questions.question: Are the banner's reasons for one console real differences, or padding like being a bit shorter?
questions.why: The summary banner explicitly contrasts the number of reasons to choose each console, providing a quick metric to justify a selection.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally weigh the overall summary of advantages before diving into the specific reasons.
questions.check: How many advantages does the banner list for each console, and do any of those specific listed reasons amount to trivial differences (e.g., dimensions) rather than functional ones?
questions.say_example: The banner gives <one console> <8> reasons and <the other> <3>. Two of the eight are just being shorter and narrower.

questions.question: Do this part's specs and included pieces match what you need?
questions.why: Reviewing details like the ceramic composition, pad dimensions, and included mounting hardware ensures the product fits your vehicle and performance criteria.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally verify the technical specifications and included hardware to decide if this product belongs on your shortlist.
questions.check: Does what the page lists for this product, specs, included parts, rated categories and eligibility lines, match every requirement the person named?
questions.say_example: This one is <semi-metallic>, and you asked for ceramic. Leaving it out.

questions.question: Does the page say another part is needed with this one?
questions.why: The product information for the Bosch brake pads explicitly states 'Replace your rotors', suggesting that buying just the pads might not be sufficient for a proper repair.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might just buy the requested brake pads and ignore the mechanical advice, leaving the user with an incomplete repair job.
questions.check: Does the product page include a warning like 'Replace your rotors' or similar text implying an additional required part beyond the one selected?
questions.say_example: The page says 'Replace your rotors' alongside these pads. On their own they may not be the whole repair.

questions.question: Is it really in stock on its own page, as the list said?
questions.why: Search indexes often lag, showing items as available in the list view that are actually out of stock or backordered when you click through to the product page.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the time wasted evaluating and shortlisting a candidate that cannot actually be purchased right now.
questions.check: Does the product's detail page show it out of stock or backordered, even though the filtered list view showed it as available?
questions.say_example: The list said in stock. The product page says <backordered, ships in 3 weeks>.

questions.question: How many servings, and how long does it keep?
questions.why: Checking the product images for details like the 49 servings and 10-year shelf life ensures the item meets your specific quantity and storage constraints.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the ability to visually verify crucial product specifications directly from the manufacturer's packaging images.
questions.check: What serving count and shelf-life figure does the product's image or description show?
questions.say_example: Read the product images, <30 servings> and a <25-year> shelf life

questions.question: Right before you decide, do the specs still show everything you need?
questions.why: Clicking the specifications tab lets you re-verify the technical details you previously reviewed to ensure they meet your strict constraints.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally double-check the exact hardware specifications before making a final decision.
questions.check: Re-reading the specs tab now, right before the pick, does every stated must-have constraint still show as met on the page?
questions.say_example: Before you decide, I read the specs again. Still a match on <the RAM> and <the battery size>.

questions.question: Does the page say you've bought this before?
questions.why: The banner explicitly states "Purchased 3 times. Last purchased [date]", which might change your decision to buy more if you are looking for new items or already have enough.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might ignore the purchase history banner and buy redundant items that you already have plenty of in your pantry.
questions.check: Does the product page show a 'Purchased before' or reorder banner indicating the person has bought this item previously?
questions.say_example: The page says you've bought this <twice> before, most recently <last spring>.

questions.question: Can this be returned if you change your mind?
questions.why: Grocery and emergency food items are often strictly non-returnable, making the purchase a final commitment with no reversal option.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to verify the return policy on a large, expensive consumable item before making a non-reversible payment.
questions.check: Does the product or policy page state that this item is non-returnable or final-sale?
questions.say_example: This one is marked <non-returnable>. No refund if you change your mind.

questions.question: Does the label photo show anything added that you didn't want?
questions.why: The product images reveal that the powder contains added cane sugar and fructose, meaning it is not pure honey.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally inspect the ingredient label to catch unwanted additives before making a purchase.
questions.check: Do the product's photos of the ingredient label show any additive (e.g., added sugar) that would make the product not meet a stated purity requirement (e.g., 'pure honey')?
questions.say_example: The label photo lists <added cane sugar>. The title says pure honey, and the label says otherwise.

questions.question: Do the height and price on the page fit the scale and budget you gave?
questions.why: Verifying the 3.54-inch height, the $9.27 price for 20 pieces, and the product images ensures the item actually fits your N scale layout and quality standards.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might rely solely on the text specifications and miss the subjective visual inspection of the product images to determine if the off-brand quality is visually acceptable.
questions.verify_form: The agent judged the trees fit on scale, price and looks - check what it read; the height in centimetres is what says the scale, and the photos are what say the quality.
questions.check: What height and price does the page show for this item, and do both fit the scale and price limit the person asked for?
questions.say_example: This one is <4 cm> tall. Your scale needs <about 2 cm>, so it's too big.

questions.question: Who is the seller behind the lowest price, and what's their rating and return policy?
questions.why: The cheapest option in a comparison might be from a newly launched third-party seller with no reviews or a restrictive return policy, which is a common risk on major retail platforms.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the protection of evaluating the seller's trustworthiness, risking counterfeit goods or a difficult return process.
questions.check: For the third-party seller offering the lowest price, what star rating and return policy does their seller page show?
questions.say_example: The seller with the lowest price is rated <3.2 stars> with a <no-returns> policy.

questions.question: Is this rating for this exact version, or pooled across colors and sizes?
questions.why: Retailers often lump reviews for all colors, sizes, or previous generations of a product together, inflating the rating of a potentially flawed specific variant.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the critical context needed to realize the high rating doesn't apply to the exact model they shortlisted.
questions.check: Does the product page include text disclosing that its rating or review count is combined across colors, sizes, or other variants rather than being specific to this one?
questions.say_example: This rating is pooled across <every color and size>. The page says so in small print under the stars.

questions.question: Do owners' reviews mention a problem the spec table doesn't?
questions.why: Reading comments from users like "[handle]" and "[handle]" provides real-world context to the technical specs shown at the top of the screen.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally weigh the subjective experiences and specific nuances shared by actual users.
questions.verify_form: The agent read the owner opinions or skipped them - check which; the specs table says nothing about glass backs breaking.
questions.check: Do the owner reviews or comments on the page mention a real-world issue (e.g., a durability or reliability problem) that the specs table doesn't cover?
questions.say_example: Owners say <the glass back cracks easily>. The spec table says nothing about that.

questions.question: Is there a full review and video beyond the key-features list?
questions.why: The screen presents both a quick list of hardware specs and an in-depth video review, meaning you must choose how much detail is necessary for your comparison.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the personal judgment of whether a quick glance at the specs is sufficient to evaluate the phone or if a deeper qualitative review is required.
questions.verify_form: The agent scanned the key features or read the full review - check which; the video and the long text were skipped in the recording.
questions.check: Does the page offer a longer video or full written review beyond the quick key-features list?
questions.say_example: Read the key-features list; skipped the <video review> and the long write-up

children.label: Total the price with shipping and fees

questions.question: Does the truck icon confirm this part ships from the same warehouse as what's already in your cart, so you're not paying an extra shipping fee?
questions.why: Hovering over the small truck icon next to the item reveals a tooltip confirming it could ship from the same location as your cart items, which saves money on shipping fees.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to strategically select parts that ship from the same location to minimize your overall shipping costs.
questions.check: Does hovering the truck icon next to this item show a tooltip confirming it ships from the same warehouse as an item already in the cart?
questions.say_example: The truck icon says this ships from the same warehouse as what's in your cart. No second shipping fee.

questions.question: Is the delivery location set to where you want this shipped?
questions.why: The Amazon navigation bar explicitly shows 'Deliver to [name] [number]', which dictates the stock availability, shipping costs, and delivery estimates shown in the search results.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might search using a default or outdated zip code, resulting in a shortlist of products that are out of stock or delayed for the user's actual location.
questions.check: Does the page's delivery-location indicator (e.g., 'Deliver to...') show the correct address or ZIP for where the person actually wants this shipped?
questions.say_example: The delivery location is set to <somewhere else>, and prices and stock follow it. Setting it to yours.

questions.question: What's the price up front once the core charge is added?
questions.why: The screen displays a base price, a separate core charge, and a combined total, indicating that the initial out-of-pocket cost is higher than the base price alone.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses visibility into the true upfront cost and the mechanics of core charge refunds when comparing part prices.
questions.check: What base price and core charge does the page show separately, and what combined total do they add up to?
questions.say_example: There's a <$34.50> core charge on top of the <$52.99> price, so it's <$87.49> up front.

questions.question: Who pays to ship the old part back, and by when?
questions.why: The core charge refund depends on returning the old part, so the cost of return shipping and the deadline dictate whether the refund is actually worth pursuing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to factor the return shipping logistics and costs into their comparison between a new part and a remanufactured one.
questions.check: Does the page's core-charge policy text state who pays return shipping for the old part and what the deadline is to send it back?
questions.say_example: The core policy says <you pay return shipping> and you have <45 days> to send the old part back.

questions.question: With the pickup fee added, is this still the better buy than the one you passed on?
questions.why: The summary of charges reveals a $3.00 fee for store pickup that brings the total to $100.95, which you must review before selecting a payment method from the dropdown.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step removes your visibility into final added costs like the pickup fee and your control over which payment method is used.
questions.check: Once the pickup fee shown in the payment summary is added, does the total still come out lower (or otherwise still winning) than the alternative(s) the person passed on?
questions.say_example: With the <$4> pickup fee, this comes to <$118.40>. That's now <$2> more than the one you passed on.

questions.question: Does the tax-free banner actually appear on the homepage, or is that promotion missing?
questions.why: Relying on a promotion requires it to actually exist, but the right column of the homepage only shows a green area instead of the asserted tax-free banner.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the visual verification needed to ensure they aren't basing their purchase on a hallucinated or missing promotion.
questions.check: Does the homepage's promotional area actually display the tax-free (or other advertised) banner, or is that space empty or showing something else?
questions.say_example: The tax-free banner isn't on the homepage. That spot is <empty>, so I'm not counting on the promotion.

questions.question: Once shipping is calculated, does the total still fit your budget?
questions.why: Filling out the address information fields and clicking the 'Calculate Shipping' button allows you to see the exact delivery fees added to the subtotal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the chance to personally review the shipping fees and confirm that the final total still fits your budget.
questions.check: After the shipping calculation runs, does the subtotal-plus-shipping total exceed the budget figure the person stated?
questions.say_example: With shipping, the total is <$214>. That's <$14> over your <$200>. OK to go over, or should I find a cheaper one?

questions.question: Can this one actually ship to you?
questions.why: A product might win the comparison on price and specs, but fail at the last mile if the retailer cannot ship it to your specific zip code or requires a distant in-store pickup.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to verify logistical feasibility before committing to a choice, potentially forcing a restart of the entire task if the agent picks an undeliverable item.
questions.check: At checkout or on the shipping-options section, does the page show a shipping restriction or unavailability message for the person's location for this specific product?
questions.say_example: This one won't ship to you. The page says <in-store pickup only>, and the nearest store is <50 miles> away.

questions.question: How does the combo pack's price compare with the single items on the grid?
questions.why: The screen shows the Dairy and Egg Combo priced at $195.99 among other Augason Farms products, letting you weigh its cost against the alternatives.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to rely on your own memory of past price drops to realize this is a rare deal worth grabbing.
questions.check: What price does the page show for the multi-pack or combo, and how does that compare with the single items still on the same grid?
questions.say_example: Priced the combo at <$142.50> against <$40 to $95> for the single items

children.label: Open the tracker on the product

children.label: Read the low, high and current

questions.question: How does the current price compare to the item's historical highs and lows?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally assess the price volatility and decide if you should buy now or wait for a price drop.

questions.question: Which time window is the price chart showing?
questions.why: Viewing the 'All Time' price history chart provides essential context on whether the current price is genuinely a good deal or just a normal fluctuation.

questions.say_example: The chart was on <3 months>. I switched it to all time to show the real highs and lows.

questions.question: Which seller's price line is being read?
questions.why: The chart displays distinct price lines for Amazon, third-party new, and third-party used sellers, allowing you to evaluate the deal based on who is actually selling the item.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to prioritize the specific seller type you trust most, as an agent might just evaluate the lowest overall price regardless of whether it is new, used, or from a third party.
questions.verify_form: The agent read one seller's line - check which; the site's own line and the third-party lines have different lows.
questions.check: Does the price-history chart show separate lines for different sellers (e.g., the retailer's own vs. third-party new or used), and do those lines have meaningfully different lows or highs?
questions.say_example: The chart has one line for <the store itself> and one for <other sellers>. The other sellers' low is <$20> lower.

questions.why: The price tracker includes a 'Remove Extreme Values' toggle, which filters out anomalous price spikes that could distort your perception of the item's average cost.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might evaluate the current discount against an artificially inflated historical high, falsely concluding that the current deal is better than it actually is.
questions.verify_form: The agent left or ticked the remove-extreme-values box - check which; the all-time high may be an outlier.

questions.verify_form: The agent trusted the comparison facts - check whether it noticed the report-as-wrong links; the data is crowd-edited.
questions.check: Does the comparison page show 'report as wrong' or similar edit/flag links next to its stated facts, indicating the data is crowd-edited rather than site-verified?
questions.say_example: These facts carry 'report as wrong' links. Anyone can edit them, so I'm treating them as unverified.

children.label: Check the rows are the same product

questions.question: Are the columns the exact versions you meant to compare, same storage, color and condition?
questions.why: Automated comparison tools sometimes pull in the base model or a different configuration than the one selected, skewing the side-by-side evaluation.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user cannot easily glance at the table headers to ensure the agent is comparing the correct configurations, risking a decision based on mismatched data.
questions.check: Do the comparison table's column headers specify the exact variant (storage, color, condition, generation) the person meant to compare, or could a different configuration have been substituted?
questions.say_example: I can't tell if these two columns are the same product. One may be a different <storage size>. Which version did you mean?

children.label: Settle on the pick
children.note: 7.1 shows up in the seven keepers that say a verdict. 7.2 shows up in wagd, where the run ends without picking an item. 7.3 and 7.4 in TTzY and IW59, the two cart runs. 7.5 in TTzY alone, where everything past the payment summary happens after the task is done. 7.6 in the keepers that leave the comparison page without picking an item.

children.label: State the pick and its reason

questions.question: Is this row really the lowest price for the first book, or is a cheaper one right above it?
questions.why: The price comparison table shows that the new copy from Weber at $30.35 is significantly cheaper than the alternatives from Half and Amazon.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the satisfaction of personally reviewing the comparison table to ensure you are getting the best possible deal on your course materials.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked a vendor row for the first book - check the row above it; the recording called the new copy the best price with the used copy cheaper directly above.
questions.check: Among the vendor rows for this book, is the row about to be called 'best price' actually the lowest price, or does a cheaper same-condition row sit elsewhere in the table?
questions.say_example: The row right above is <75 cents> cheaper for the same condition. That's the better price.

questions.question: For the second book, cheaper and slower, or pricier and faster?
questions.why: The price comparison block presents multiple options varying by price, condition, retailer, and delivery time, requiring a specific tradeoff.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally balance your budget against your tolerance for used conditions and longer shipping times.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked a row for the second book on price, condition and delivery time - check the three; the cheapest row ships in three weeks.
questions.check: Do the candidate rows for this book differ in a way that trades price against shipping time (e.g., the cheapest option ships slowest), such that no single row wins on both?
questions.say_example: The cheapest one ships in <2 weeks>. A pricier one arrives in <3 days>. Which matters more, price or speed?

questions.question: Is this row really cheaper for the third book than the store's own used copy?
questions.why: The price comparison block displays multiple offers requiring a trade-off between price, condition, and delivery speed, such as cheap used copies taking 21 days versus a new Amazon copy arriving in 5 days.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally weigh your urgency for the book against your willingness to buy a used copy to save money.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked a row for the third book - check it against the store's used row; the recording called an Amazon row cheaper when it was not.
questions.check: Is the retailer row about to be called cheaper for this book actually cheaper than the alternative rows shown, or does another row (e.g., the store's own used copy) beat it?
questions.say_example: That row isn't the cheapest. The store's own used copy beside it is priced lower.

questions.question: Is the part with the popularity heart really the better buy, or just the one people order most?
questions.why: The red heart icon indicating it is a popular part provides social proof that might justify the $22.99 price over cheaper options.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to weigh whether a popularity indicator justifies paying a higher price than the cheaper alternatives.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked the pad with the popularity heart over cheaper rows - check its reason; the heart is the site's count, not a spec.
questions.check: Is the item marked with a popularity badge or heart actually the cheapest and fullest-featured option, or do other rows offer a lower price and more listed specs?
questions.say_example: The heart is on the pricier one, and a cheaper row lists more specs. The heart only means people order it a lot.

questions.question: Is there a single-unit option to try before buying the case?
questions.why: The narrator suggests buying just one can to try it out as a hedge against expected price increases, rather than committing to a bulk purchase immediately.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the strategic advice to sample a small quantity of a product to verify quality before committing more money in a volatile market.
questions.verify_form: The agent bought one unit or more - check the quantity; the narrator's advice was one can to test before buying more.
questions.check: Does the product page or listing offer both a single-unit and a bulk or case purchase option, with prices for each?
questions.say_example: There's a single can at <$4> as well as the case at <$22>. You could try one before the whole case.

questions.question: What target price should you set for the price drop alert?
questions.why: Entering a realistic desired price below the current $10.66 ensures you only receive an email notification when a meaningful discount occurs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally weigh how much of a discount is worth delaying the purchase for.
questions.verify_form: The agent set a target price for the alert - check the figure; the presets were percentages off the current price and the recording typed its own.
questions.check: What percentage-off presets does the price-alert form offer, and what is the current price they're calculated from?
questions.say_example: The alert wants a target price. The presets are <5, 10 or 15 percent> off today's <$14.20>. What price should I set?

questions.question: Did the price watch save?
questions.why: Confirming the green checkmark and success message ensures the tracker is active, meaning you won't have to manually check the retailer's site every day for a price drop.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate peace of mind that comes from personally verifying the price alert was successfully registered.
questions.check: Does the page show a success confirmation (e.g., a checkmark or 'Success' message) after submitting the price watch?
questions.say_example: Saved the price watch; the page showed <a green checkmark and Success>

children.label: Add the pick to the cart

questions.question: Should the small add-on the site offers go in the order too?
questions.why: The screen shows an info popup detailing a 5-pack of random collector magnets for $1.25, presenting an optional novelty add-on.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to make a spontaneous, personal choice about purchasing a fun, low-cost novelty item.
questions.verify_form: The agent added or skipped the magnet pack - check which; it is an add-on to the order, not one of the candidates.
questions.check: Does a popup or info panel offer an optional add-on item (e.g., a small novelty pack) unrelated to the compared candidates?
questions.say_example: The site is offering an add-on, <a small novelty pack> for <$2>. It's not one of the things you were comparing, so I'm skipping it.

questions.question: Is it set to a subscription instead of a one-time purchase?
questions.why: Retailers frequently pre-select options like 'Subscribe & Save' to advertise a lower upfront price, hiding the commitment of recurring deliveries in a small, easily overlooked radio button.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user risks being enrolled in an unwanted ongoing subscription because they cannot visually catch that the lowest price is tied to a recurring order.
questions.check: Is the 'Subscribe & Save' or recurring-delivery option pre-selected by default, rather than the one-time purchase option?
questions.say_example: It's defaulted to <Subscribe & Save>, which is a repeat order. Switching it to one-time.

children.label: Verify the cart matches the pick

questions.question: Check out with just this in the cart, or keep browsing?
questions.why: The cart shows the Bosch brake pads for $22.99, requiring a decision to either finalize the order or return to the catalog.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the control to decide whether to finalize the current selection or continue browsing for additional items.
questions.verify_form: The agent went to checkout or kept shopping with one item in the cart - check which; more items may change the shipping.
questions.check: How many items does the cart hold, and what subtotal does it show, before checkout?
questions.say_example: Checked the cart, <1 item> at <$31.40>, before checkout

questions.question: Does the cart hold only what was added just now?
questions.why: An unexplained jump in the cart's item count and subtotal between moments indicates that products were added off-screen, breaking the continuity of the selection process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses oversight of their final purchase and budget if the agent adds unapproved items to the cart without showing the comparison and selection process.
questions.check: Does the cart's item count or subtotal include anything beyond what was explicitly added during this comparison session, e.g., an unexplained jump in count or total?
questions.say_example: The cart went from <2 items, $45> to <3 items, $68> without anything added on screen. The extra one isn't from this session.

questions.question: Do you want to take over at the sign-in or payment form?
questions.why: The screen shows a payment-method dropdown and empty credit card fields, requiring a decision on whether to expose sensitive financial data to finalize the purchase.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The delegator loses control over their sensitive financial information and the final authorization of the actual purchase.
questions.verify_form: The agent entered payment details or stopped - check which; the recording stops on the empty card form.
questions.check: Is a sign-in form asking for the person's password, or a payment form asking for card details, now on screen, so that going further means entering the person's own details?
questions.say_example: This screen wants your <password or card details> to finish the order. That's yours to type. Take it from here, or should I stop?

questions.question: Do you have the Student ID the tax-free deal needs?
questions.why: The checkout screen displays a banner stating 'TAX FREE* Shopping... *Student ID required', making the discount conditional on having specific identification.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might calculate the budget assuming the tax-free discount applies, only for the user to be charged tax because they cannot produce the required Student ID.
questions.check: Does the checkout page's tax-free promotion banner require a Student ID or other credential the person may not have on hand?
questions.say_example: The tax-free saving needs a <Student ID> at checkout. If you don't have one, count on the full price.

questions.question: Does the final screen show a backorder or delay that wasn't there before?
questions.why: Search results and comparison tables often show items as available, but the final selection step reveals a months-long lead time that violates the buyer's timeline.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to catch a delayed delivery schedule before finalizing the purchase, potentially missing a deadline.
questions.check: Does the final checkout or selection screen show a backorder notice or delayed ship date that wasn't shown earlier in the comparison?
questions.say_example: This screen says <backordered, 6 to 8 weeks>. The comparison page didn't show that.
